column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 48: “There are four traits: whoever has them is a hypocrite”

column2: From ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr (may Allah be pleased with them both), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “There are four traits: whoever has them is a hypocrite,

and whoever has one of them has a trait of hypocrisy until he gives it up: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks his promise; when he disputes, he acts wickedly; and when he makes a covenant, he betrays it.” Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded it.
Both al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded this hadith in the two Ṣaḥīḥs through the narration of al-Aʿmash, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Murrah, from Masrūq, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ.

They also recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The sign of the hypocrite is three things: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks his promise; and when he is entrusted with something, he betrays the trust.”
In a narration of Muslim's: “even if he fasts and prays and claims to be a Muslim”; and in another narration of his: “Among the signs of the hypocrite are three.”
This has also been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by other routes.

Some of those who lean towards irjāʾ [the doctrine of the Murjiʾah] took this hadith to refer to the hypocrites of the Prophet's time ﷺ: they spoke to the Prophet ﷺ and lied to him, he entrusted them with his secret and they betrayed him,

and they promised him that they would go out with him on campaign and broke their promise. Muḥammad al-Muḥrim narrated this interpretation from ʿAṭāʾ, saying that ʿAṭāʾ said: Jābir told it to me from the Prophet ﷺ; and he mentioned that al-Ḥasan came round to this view of ʿAṭāʾ's when it reached him.
This is a lie. Al-Muḥrim is a lying shaykh, known for lying.
It has been narrated from ʿAṭāʾ by two other, weak routes that he objected to al-Ḥasan's saying, “Three things: whoever has them is a hypocrite,” and said: The brothers of Yūsuf spoke and lied,

promised and broke their promise, were entrusted and betrayed, and yet they were not hypocrites. This is not authentic from ʿAṭāʾ; and al-Ḥasan did not say this of his own accord, but because it had reached him from the Prophet ﷺ.

The hadith, then, is firmly established from him ﷺ, with no doubt that it is established and authentic. The people of knowledge whose views carry weight explain it as follows. Hypocrisy (nifāq), in the language, belongs to the same family as deception and cunning, showing good outwardly while concealing the opposite; and in the Sharīʿah it divides into two kinds.
The first is the greater hypocrisy: that a person outwardly shows faith in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers and the Last Day, while inwardly holding what contradicts all or part of that.

This is the hypocrisy that existed in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. The Qurʾān was revealed censuring those who held it and declaring them disbelievers, and it told that they are in the lowest depth of the Fire.
The second is the lesser hypocrisy, the hypocrisy of deeds: that a person shows a righteous outward appearance while concealing inwardly what is contrary to it.
The roots of this hypocrisy go back to the traits mentioned in these hadiths, and they are five. The first is to tell something to someone who believes you, while you are lying to him.
In the Musnad, the Prophet ﷺ said: “It is a great betrayal that you tell your brother something in which he believes you, while you are lying to him.”

Al-Ḥasan said: It used to be said: Hypocrisy is a difference between the private and the public, between word and deed, and between the way one goes in and the way one comes out. And it used to be said: The foundation of hypocrisy, on which hypocrisy is built, is lying.
The second: when he promises, he breaks his promise. This is of two kinds.

The first is to make a promise while intending not to keep it. This is the worst kind of breaking a promise. Even if one says, “I will do such-and-such, if Allah the Exalted wills,” while intending not to do it, it is a lie and a broken promise; al-Awzāʿī said this.
The second is to make a promise intending to keep it, then change one's mind and break it with no excuse for breaking it.
Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “When a man makes a promise intending to keep it, and then does not keep it, there is no sin on him.”
Al-Tirmidhī said: Its chain is not strong.
Al-Ismāʿīlī and others recorded it from the hadith of Salmān: ʿAlī met Abū Bakr and ʿUmar and said: Why do I see you both so heavy-hearted?
They said: Because of a hadith we heard from the Prophet ﷺ, in which he mentioned the traits of the hypocrite:
“When he promises, he breaks his promise; when he speaks, he lies; and when he is entrusted, he betrays.” Which of us is safe from these traits?
ʿAlī went in to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned this to him, and he said: “I did tell them that, but I did not mean it in the way you are taking it.

Rather, the hypocrite is the one who, when he speaks, is telling himself that he will lie; when he promises, is telling himself that he will break it; and when he is entrusted, is telling himself that he will betray.”
Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī said of this hadith, in the narrations of Salmān and Zayd ibn Arqam:
The two hadiths are inconsistent (muḍṭarib), and there are unknown narrators in both chains.
Al-Dāraquṭnī said: The hadith is not established. And Allah knows best.

Al-Ṭabarānī and al-Ismāʿīlī recorded, from the hadith of ʿAlī as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ): “A promise is a debt. Woe to whoever promises and then breaks it” — he said it three times. Its chain contains an unknown narrator. It is also narrated from the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, who said:

None of you should promise his child something and then not give it to him, for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “A promise is a gift.” Its chain is open to question, though its first part is authentic from Ibn Masʿūd as his own words.
Among the mursal reports of al-Ḥasan, the Prophet ﷺ said: “A promise is a present.”
In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, from a freed slave of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿah, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿah, who said:

The Prophet ﷺ came to our house when I was a boy, and I went out to play. My mother said: ʿAbdullāh, come here and I will give you something. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “What did you mean to give him?”
She said: I meant to give him a date. He said: “Had you not done so, a lie would have been written against you.”
The printed text reads قلتُ (“I said”); read قالت (“she said”), as the reply is the mother's and as Abū Dāwūd and the other sources have it. The Abū al-Nūr edition has the same misprint.
Its chain contains someone who is not known.
Al-Zuhrī mentioned from Abū Hurayrah, who said: Whoever says to a child, “Come, here is a date,” and then gives him nothing, it is a lie.

The scholars have disagreed over whether keeping a promise is obligatory. Some hold it obligatory without qualification; al-Bukhārī mentioned in his Ṣaḥīḥ that Ibn al-Ashwaʿ gave judgement that promises must be kept,

and this is the view of a group of the Ẓāhirīs and others. Some hold it obligatory to keep a promise when it has led the one promised to incur a loss; this is what is reported from Mālik. Many jurists do not hold it obligatory at all.

The third: when he disputes, he acts wickedly. By wickedness (fujūr) is meant deliberately departing from the truth, so that truth becomes falsehood and falsehood truth. Lying is one of the things that leads to this,
as he ﷺ said: “Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness, and wickedness leads to the Fire.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from the Prophet ﷺ: “The most hateful of men to Allah is the fiercely quarrelsome adversary.”

He ﷺ also said: “You bring your disputes to me, and perhaps some of you are more eloquent in presenting their case than others. I judge only according to what I hear; so if I give someone a judgement for something that is his brother's right, let him not take it, for I am only cutting off for him a piece of the Fire.”
He ﷺ also said: “Some eloquence is magic.”

So if a man is able, in a dispute — whether over religion or over worldly matters — to champion falsehood, make the listener imagine it is true, weaken the truth and present it in the guise of falsehood, that is one of the foulest of prohibited things

and one of the vilest traits of hypocrisy. In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, from Ibn ʿUmar, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever disputes on behalf of falsehood, knowing it to be so, remains under Allah's displeasure until he desists.”
In another narration of his: “And whoever helps in a dispute unjustly has incurred wrath from Allah.”

The fourth: when he makes a covenant, he betrays it and does not fulfil it. Allah has commanded that covenants be fulfilled, saying: “Fulfil the covenant; the covenant will be asked about” [al-Isrāʾ 17:34]; and: “Fulfil the covenant of Allah when you have made a covenant, and do not break oaths after confirming them, when you have made Allah a surety over you” [al-Naḥl 16:91];

and: “Those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price will have no share in the Hereafter. Allah will not speak to them or look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and they will have a painful punishment” [Āl ʿImrān 3:77].
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Ibn ʿUmar, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every betrayer will have a banner on the Day of Resurrection by which he will be known.”

In one narration: “A banner will be raised for the betrayer on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: Behold, this is the betrayal of so-and-so.” Both also recorded something with the same meaning from the hadith of Anas.
Muslim recorded from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Every betrayer will have a banner at his backside on the Day of Resurrection.”
Betrayal is unlawful in every covenant between a Muslim and anyone else, even if the party to the covenant is a disbeliever. That is why, in the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr,

the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever kills a person under a covenant (muʿāhad) without due right will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance can be found from a distance of forty years.” Al-Bukhārī recorded it.
Allah the Exalted has commanded in His Book that covenants with the idolaters be fulfilled, so long as they keep to their covenants and break nothing of them.
As for covenants among Muslims, keeping them is still more binding, and breaking them a greater sin.
One of the gravest is breaking the pledge to the ruler (imām) by someone who has pledged allegiance to him and accepted him. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said:

“There are three to whom Allah will not speak on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them, and they will have a painful punishment” — and among them he mentioned: “a man who pledged allegiance to a ruler only for worldly gain: if he gives him what he wants, he keeps faith with him, and if not, he does not.”

The covenants that must be kept and in which betrayal is unlawful include all the contracts Muslims make among themselves when they have agreed to them by mutual consent — sales, marriages and other binding contracts that must be fulfilled —
and likewise whatever must be fulfilled for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, of what the servant pledges to his Lord, such as a vow of devotion (nadhr al-tabarrur) and the like.

The fifth: betraying a trust. When a man is entrusted with something, he must render it, as the Exalted said: “Allah commands you to render trusts to those to whom they are due” [al-Nisāʾ 4:58]; and the Prophet ﷺ said: “Render the trust to the one who entrusted you.”

In his sermon at the Farewell Pilgrimage he said: “Whoever has a trust with him, let him render it to the one who entrusted him with it.” And the Mighty and Majestic said: “O you who believe, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor knowingly betray your trusts” [al-Anfāl 8:27]. Betraying a trust is thus one of the traits of hypocrisy.

In the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, as his own words — it has also been narrated as marfūʿ: “Being killed in the path of Allah expiates every sin except the trust. The holder of the trust will be brought and told: Render your trust. He will say: How, my Lord, when the world has gone?

It will be said: Take him to al-Hāwiyah [the Abyss]. He will be cast down into it until he reaches its bottom, and there he will find it in the form it had. He will pick it up, put it on his neck and climb with it through the fire of Hell, until, when he sees that he has come out of it,
it slips and falls, and he falls after it for ever and ever.” He said: There is trust in the prayer, trust in fasting and trust in speech, and the gravest of these is deposits.
It is narrated of Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī that he derived the content of this hadith — I mean the hadith “The sign of the hypocrite is three” — from the Qurʾān,
saying: The confirmation of this is in the Book of Allah the Exalted: “When the hypocrites come to you, they say: We bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah” up to His words:

“and Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are liars” [al-Munāfiqūn 63:1]. The Exalted also said: “And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah: If He gives us of His bounty…” up to His words: “So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the day they meet Him, because they broke what they had promised Allah and because they used to lie” [al-Tawbah 9:75–77].

And He said: “We offered the trust to the heavens, the earth and the mountains…” up to His words: “so that Allah may punish the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women” [al-Aḥzāb 33:72–73]. Something similar to these words has been narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, after which he recited His words: “So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts…” to the end of the verse.

The upshot is that all of the lesser hypocrisy comes back to a difference between the inward and the outward; al-Ḥasan said this. Al-Ḥasan also said: Part of hypocrisy is a difference between heart and tongue, between the private and the public, and between the way one goes in and the way one comes out.

A group of the Salaf said: The humility of hypocrisy is that you see the body humble while the heart is not humble. The meaning of this has been narrated from ʿUmar, and it is narrated that he said on the pulpit: What I fear most for you is the knowledgeable hypocrite. They said: How can a hypocrite be knowledgeable?
He said: He speaks wisdom and acts unjustly — or he said: acts wrongly.
Ḥudhayfah was asked about the hypocrite and said: He is the one who describes faith and does not act on it.
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Ibn ʿUmar: He was told: We go in to our rulers and say to them the opposite of what we say when we have left them. He said: We used to count this as hypocrisy.
In the Musnad, from Ḥudhayfah, who said: You speak words that we used to count as hypocrisy in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. In one narration he said:
A man would speak a word in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and become a hypocrite by it, and I hear it from one of you ten times a day in a single sitting.
Bilāl ibn Saʿd said: The hypocrite says what he knows to be right and does what he knows to be wrong.
That is why the Companions feared hypocrisy for themselves, and ʿUmar used to ask Ḥudhayfah about himself.
Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī was asked: Did those of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ whom you met fear hypocrisy?
He said: Yes. Praise be to Allah, I met a good number of them — yes, intensely; yes, intensely.
Al-Bukhārī said in his Ṣaḥīḥ: Ibn Abī Mulaykah said: I met thirty of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, every one of whom feared hypocrisy for himself.
It is mentioned that al-Ḥasan said: None fears it but a believer, and none feels safe from it but a hypocrite. End of quotation.
It is narrated that al-Ḥasan swore: No believer has ever passed away, or remained, without fearing hypocrisy; and no hypocrite has ever passed away, or remained, without feeling safe from hypocrisy.
He used to say: Whoever does not fear hypocrisy is a hypocrite.
A man heard Abū al-Dardāʾ seeking refuge from hypocrisy in his prayer, and when he had given the salām, he said to him: What have you to do with hypocrisy?
He said: O Allah, forgive! — three times. Do not feel safe from trial. By Allah, a man may be put to trial in a single hour and turn back from his religion.
The reports from the Salaf on this are very many.
Sufyān al-Thawrī said: We differ from the Murjiʾah on three points. Among them he mentioned: We say there is hypocrisy, and they say there is no hypocrisy.
Al-Awzāʿī said: ʿUmar feared hypocrisy for himself. He was told: They say

it was not that ʿUmar feared he was a hypocrite at that time, so that he asked Ḥudhayfah; rather, he feared he would be tried with it before he died. He said: This is the view of the people of innovation.
He was indicating that ʿUmar feared hypocrisy for himself in the present. It appears that he meant that ʿUmar feared for himself, in the present, the lesser hypocrisy;

and the lesser hypocrisy is a means and a pathway to the greater, just as sins are the courier of disbelief. Just as it is feared that one who persists in sin will be stripped of faith at death, so it is feared that one who persists in the traits of hypocrisy will be stripped of faith and become an outright hypocrite.
Imam Aḥmad was asked: What do you say of someone who does not fear hypocrisy for himself?
He said: And who can feel safe from hypocrisy for himself?
Al-Ḥasan used to call anyone in whom the traits of practical hypocrisy appeared a hypocrite, and something similar is narrated from Ḥudhayfah.
Al-Shaʿbī said: Whoever lies is a hypocrite. Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī reported this view from a group of the hadith scholars.

The disagreement reported from Imam Aḥmad and others about the one who commits major sins has already been mentioned near the beginning of the book: is he called a disbeliever, with a disbelief that does not take him out of the religion, or not?
The name “disbelief” is weightier than the name “hypocrisy”, and perhaps this is what ʿAṭāʾ objected to in al-Ḥasan, if that is authentically reported from him.
One of the gravest traits of practical hypocrisy is for a person to do a deed and make it appear that he intended good by it, when he did it only to reach some evil aim of his;
he achieves it, reaches his aim through this deception, and rejoices in his cunning and deceit and in people's praise of him for what he showed outwardly,
having reached through it the evil aim he concealed. Allah has related this in the Qurʾān of the hypocrites and of the Jews. Of the hypocrites He related that they

“took a mosque for harm and disbelief, to divide the believers and as a station for one who had fought Allah and His Messenger before; and they will surely swear: We intended nothing but good. Allah bears witness that they are liars” [al-Tawbah 9:107].

And about the Jews He revealed: “Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought about and love to be praised for what they have not done — do not think them safe from the punishment; they will have a painful punishment” [Āl ʿImrān 3:188]. This verse was revealed about the Jews: the Prophet ﷺ asked them about something, and they concealed it

and told him something else. They went out having made him think they had told him what he had asked about, sought praise for that, and rejoiced at what they had brought about by concealing what they had been asked. Ibn ʿAbbās said this, and his hadith is recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs.
Both also have, from Abū Saʿīd, that it was revealed about men among the hypocrites who, when the Prophet ﷺ went out on campaign, stayed behind

and rejoiced at sitting at home after he had gone. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned from the campaign, they made excuses to him and swore oaths, and loved to be praised for what they had not done.
In the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever cheats us is not of us, and cunning and deception are in the Fire.”
Allah has described the hypocrites as deceivers, and Abū al-ʿAtāhiyah put it well when he said:
There is no worldly life except through religion, / and religion is nothing but noble character.
Cunning and deception are in the Fire; / they are among the traits of the people of hypocrisy.

Once the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) were sure that hypocrisy is a difference between the inward and the outward, some of them feared for themselves that if their presence of heart, their tenderness and their humility on hearing the reminder changed when they went back to worldly matters and were taken up with family, children and wealth, this might be hypocrisy on their part,
as in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Ḥanẓalah al-Usaydī: He passed by Abū Bakr, weeping, and Abū Bakr said: What is wrong with you?

He said: Ḥanẓalah has become a hypocrite, Abū Bakr! We are with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he reminds us of Paradise and the Fire until it is as though we see them with our own eyes; then, when we go back,

we busy ourselves with our wives and our estates, and we forget much. Abū Bakr said: By Allah, we are the same. So they went off to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: “What is wrong with you, Ḥanẓalah?”
He said: Ḥanẓalah has become a hypocrite, Messenger of Allah; and he told him the like of what he had said to Abū Bakr. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“If you remained in the state in which you leave my presence, the angels would shake hands with you in your gatherings and on your paths. But, Ḥanẓalah, there is a time for this and a time for that.”

In the Musnad of al-Bazzār, from Anas, who said: They said: Messenger of Allah, when we are with you we are in one state, and when we leave you we are in another. He said: “How are you with your Lord?”
They said: Allah is our Lord in private and in public. He said: “That is not hypocrisy.”
It is narrated by another route from Anas, who said: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to him one morning and said: We are ruined! He said: “What is that?”
They said: Hypocrisy, hypocrisy! He said: “Do you not bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah?”
They said: Certainly. He said: “Then that is not hypocrisy.” Then he mentioned the meaning of the hadith of Ḥanẓalah given above.
